name: Azeez Afolabi
feedback: D1 is the strongest piece. You catalogued nine real findings with quoted lines and mostly correct mappings: SQL injection A03/CWE-89 with the admin' OR '1'='1 to 302 evidence, hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 CWE-798, no token expiry CWE-613, the open redirect via next CWE-601, the path traversal returning root:x:0:0 CWE-22, and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite CWE-614. Small slips that I let stand as defensible variants: MD5 is better tagged CWE-916 than CWE-327, and alg:none is closer to CWE-347 than CWE-345. Where D1 fell down hard is the decoy. The actual safe construct in this pack is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and sound, so the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret, not the comparison. You instead labelled the stored XSS as a disproved decoy and argued it was inert, but the stored XSS is a genuine finding: capture line 02:18:47 shows the cookie beacon firing to 185.220.101.9:8443, which is execution, not a submission that went nowhere. So you lost the full six-point decoy row and half of the XSS-plus-XXE pair. D2 reads cleanly for the hops you included, with verbatim payloads and timestamps for recon 02:14:08, the failed guess 02:14:55, SQLi 02:15:31 and the 312-row pull 02:16:04 and the file read 02:24:02. You dropped the stored XSS hop at 02:18:47 and the open redirect at 02:21:13, which breaks the chain in the middle, and you did not surface the senior insight that the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, a scope change S:C. Your SQLi CVSS came out 9.8 with A:H, but the bypass does not touch availability, so the defensible vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N giving about 9.1. I did credit your honest handling of the placeholder balances in impact, where you reported the 6,400 to 950,000 range and refused to extrapolate. D3 ties findings to evidence well and has a usable threat model, but the executive summary ends on confirmed extraction rather than a plain customers-and-naira headline, it carries the same wrong decoy, and the remediation list is ordered by severity rather than by effort-to-risk, which caps that row at half. Your two detection stopgaps name the OR 1=1 tautology and /etc/passwd path watching but give no exact log field and no false-positive rate, so that row stays low. D4 cited ISC2 Canons by number and anchored to your own 312-row finding, which is good, but it only answered two of the four prompts, leaving out the colleague-with-evidence scenario and the one action you take regardless of your manager, and it named the NDPA only in general without Section 40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) or Section 41 (notify the 312 data subjects on high risk). I looked for a way to push this into the 70s and the missing chain hops, the severity-ordered remediation, the absent detection specifics and the half-answered ethics would not support it. The single most important fix: correct your decoy analysis. The hash_equals branch is the safe construct, the stored XSS is real with a live cookie beacon, and labelling a genuine vulnerability as the decoy cost you across both D1 and D3.
